title: The Word That Means Three Things: static in a Function, static in a Class, and the Counter That Forgot Copies

questions.question: What does static do to a variable declared inside a function?
options: Makes it constant
Makes it visible to other files
Makes it stored on the stack
Makes it outlive the call: it is built the first time control reaches it, once, and keeps its value between calls
questions.explanation: Three calls to a function with static int next = 1; return next++; gave 1, 2, 3. The price is that the function now has a memory.

questions.question: A global object, then two static locals reached in the order B, A. In what order are they built and destroyed?
options: Built in the order they are written, destroyed in the same order
Built when main returns, destroyed immediately
The global before main, then B and A each when its function is first called; destroyed after main, A then B, then the global
All built before main, destroyed in a random order
questions.explanation: Measured on gcc 11 and clang 14. A static local is built when first reached, once, and everything is destroyed in the reverse of the order it was built.

questions.question: A Wheel with a double radius_ and a static int count is 8 bytes. The same class with an int count kept in each object is 16. Why?
options: A static member belongs to the class and not to any object, so it takes no space in the object
The compiler optimises static members away
Static members are compressed
Static members are stored in the double
questions.explanation: One count for the whole class, wherever it lives, not one per wheel. That is also why a static member function has no this.

questions.question: A counter is incremented in a class's constructor and decremented in its destructor. One object is copied and both are destroyed. What does the counter read afterwards?
options: It depends on the optimiser
-1, because the copy was destroyed but never counted in, since the compiler's copy constructor does not touch the counter
1, since the copy keeps the count
0, since each object was counted in and out
questions.explanation: A copy is a new object that the ordinary constructor never ran for. The counter drifts down by one for every copy, so the copy constructor has to count too.

questions.question: A class declares static int live_; and nothing else, and a static function returns live_. It compiles. What happens at the link step?
options: It fails to compile, not link
It links, and live_ is zero
It fails: undefined reference to Wheel::live_, because a declaration inside the class is a promise and not a variable
It links with a warning
questions.explanation: Measured on gcc and clang. In C++17, inline static int live_ = 0; declares and defines it in one line. Before that, exactly one .cpp file needed int Wheel::live_ = 0;.

questions.question: Why can a static member function not use a member like radius_?
options: Because a static member function can be called with no object, so it has no this, and radius_ is part of an object
Because radius_ is a double
Because radius_ is private
Because static functions cannot read anything
questions.explanation: Whose radius? There is no wheel. Both compilers refuse it, which checks/ proves. An ordinary member function may use a static member, because the class-wide counter exists whichever object is asking.
